title: The meadow of piety and the good creation of irrational animals
english: The meadows of piety are beautiful—not because they are adorned with colors that fade, but because they bloom with heavenly flowers. And the flowers of piety are the fruits of a life inspired by God. For the virtues lead us up to that wonderful, original beauty that was made according to the image of God and according to his likeness. This likeness through virtue, then, does not allow us to be called a horse instead of a human being. So when we pursue it, we are no longer named wolf and dragon and snake and scorpion, dragged down into the insult of the irrational animals. Instead, we are—and are called, and are believed to be—a wonderful and precious image of God, preserving the original beauty of the stamp. You became master of the irrational animals; do not imitate the ways of your servants. Not because the irrational animals are worthless—nothing evil was created by the Good One. Let no one suppose that the irrational animals are placed in the territory of evil, just because they have been brought forward as an image of evil for those who do not live according to virtue. If that were so, how could Scripture say, “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was good”—and not simply good, but “very good” (Genesis 1:31)? Since the things that were made have been brought forward as images of evil—the lion as an image of the tyrant, the snake of the crooked and most wicked in character, the scorpion of the one who strikes, the wolf of the grasping man—where, someone says, would the things that were made be good, when they are so openly taken up as images of evil? But those who love learning must understand this: these things are not evil by their own nature, nor are they called evil. They are a condition that suits the irrational animals. But when that condition comes into a rational nature, it insults the sight and dulls rational freedom. You received, O human being, the dignity of a master. Do not pursue the dishonorable, slavish rank of the irrational animals. For you insult yourself when you imitate the savagery of the irrational animals—not because the irrational animals are evil or are called evil, but because a dishonorable and slavish image does not suit those who are free. Just as a distinguished and renowned man, if he puts on or wraps himself in a slave's garment, is insulted and disgraced—not because the clothing is worthless and filthy, but because it suits a slave and does not fit a free man—so too, if you take on the character of a scorpion and a wolf, the nature of the irrational animals is not slandered; rather, your own condition is insulted—the condition that received mastery and yet pursues the things of a slave. I have brought these points forward out of necessity, so that no one may take what has been said as an insult to creation, as though God had made something worthless. For all things are truly good, and very good, if each keeps its own order and pursues its own law. And so that you may learn, beloved, that nothing worthless by nature has been made by God, God has taught us to take an image even from these irrational animals. For he has set before us certain excellent qualities of the irrational animals to imitate, so that we may not slander what has been made as evil—not the whole nature, but only what suits a rational condition. Did you not hear today the author of Proverbs saying, “Go to the ant, you sluggard, and imitate his ways” (Proverbs 6:6)? Did you not understand how, by setting before us the diligence of the ant, he trained us toward unhesitating eagerness?

orientation: The homily opens by praising the virtues as the meadow of piety that restores the image of God, then defends the goodness of irrational animals against those who would call them evil because Scripture uses them as images of vice.
